newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Tropical timber pact set to start up next year.
newsitem.headline: Tropical timber pact set to start up next year.

text.p: Nearly 40 countries producing or using tropical timber agreed on Friday that a controversial pact to sustain forests negotiated in 1994 would go into effect from the start of next year.

The agreement came at a brief open meeting called by the United Nations' Conference of Trade and Development (UNCTAD), a major forum for discussion of the diminishing number of world commodity accords.

The pact, the International Tropical Timber Agreement (ITTA), was originally set to be in force from February last year but the timetable was scrapped when not enough countriess came on board in time.

Brazil, a strong critic of the accord which had not signed it, announced at Friday's session that it would now do so while indicating that it still felt the deal should be extended to cover temperate forests in developed countries.
As the world's third-largest producer, its participation is considered key to the pact's success.
The United States, a top consumer of tropical wood products like plywood and veneer sheets, has signed but not yet ratified -- apparently due to opposition in Congress to such accords.

Countries at the meeting, called by UNCTAD Secretary-General Rubens Ricupero at the request of the Yokohama-based International Tropical Timber Council, decided unanimously that entry into force would be on a "provisional" basis.

But UNCTAD officials said this was a device to make it easier politically for other countries to join and did not make the pact any less effective than if it had been implemented "definitively" -- another option considered.

The ITTA, which does not provide for direct market intervention, replaces an earlier 1983 agreement. World trade in tropical timber accounts for some $7.5 billion, about 10 percent of all timber trade.
Under the pact, tropical timber producers -- in Asia, Africa and Latin America -- pledge to try to export wood only from sustainably-managed forests by the year 2000.
The accord also provides for establishment of a "partnership fund" to help producing countries ensure that logging does not reduce overall forest cover.

Under its terms consumer nations, mainly industrialised economies, agreed that they would try to do the same for their own non-tropical timber exports, but resisted efforts to extend the accord to cover temperate and boreal forests.
The pact disappointed environmental groups, who were arguing for export limits as part of a campaign to combat deforestation and achieve forest sustainability by the end of the century.
This target was also set by the U.N.'s Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED), held in Rio de Janeiro at summit level in June 1992.

Representatives from some 50 countries which produce and consume all types of timber and timber products are presently meeting in Geneva to work out recommendations on preserving the world's endangered forests for another U.N. summit next year.

Producer countries who have formally now approved the ITTA are Bolivia, Burma, Cameroon, Congo, Ivory Coast, Ecuador, Gabon, Ghana, Honduras, Indonesia, Liberia, Malaysia, Panama, Papua-New Guinea, Peru, Philippines, Thailand, Togo and Zaire.

Consumer states who have ratified are Australia, Belgium, Britain, Canada, China, Denmark, Egypt, Finland, Germany, Japan, Luxemburg, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, South Korea, Spain, Sweden and Switzerland.
